query: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has high strength at room temperature and elevated temperature but a relatively high density of 10.21 g cm−3. What single intervention could reduce its density without sacrificing its mechanical properties at room temperature and at elevated temperatures, including approximately 1000 °C? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict directional changes relative to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, define the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and propose an experiment and rejection criterion that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Substitution of heavier elements with lighter ones in the HfMoTaTiZr alloy can reduce its density without sacrificing its mechanical properties at room temperature and elevated temperatures.
generation.intervention: substitution of heavier elements (e.g., Hf) with lighter ones (e.g., Ti or Zr) or adding low-density alloying elements
generation.conditions: room temperature and elevated temperatures (up to 1000 °C)
generation.mechanism: alloying and density reduction through substitution or addition of lighter elements, potentially leading to a more stable solid solution with improved mechanical properties
generation.predicted_outcome: reduced density without significant loss of mechanical strength at room and elevated temperatures
generation.baseline: as-cast HfMoTaTiZr with a density of 10.21 g cm−3
generation.boundary: temperature range: room temperature to 1000 °C; loading conditions: compressive and tensile loading
generation.uncertainty: the exact amount of density reduction and the potential effects on mechanical properties, such as strength and ductility, are uncertain and require experimental verification

falsification_experiment.design: prepare alloy samples with varying compositions (e.g., HfMoTaTiZr, Hf0.5MoTaTiZr, MoTaTiZr) and test their mechanical properties (e.g., compressive strength, tensile strength, ductility) at room temperature and elevated temperatures (up to 1000 °C)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: if the density of the modified alloy is not reduced by at least 5% compared to the as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, or if the mechanical properties (strength and ductility) are significantly compromised at room temperature or elevated temperatures, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are a relatively new class of multicomponent materials that are based on several refractory metals, but may also contain other, generally low density, elements and typically have a body centered cubic (BCC) crystal structure. These alloys have recently received much attention because of their attractive combination of properties not achievable by other classes of metallic alloys. For example, the first two RHEAs, NbMoTaW and NbMoTaVW, showed weak temperature dependence of yield strength in the temperature range from 600 °C to 1600 °C, with yield strength above 400 MPa at 1600 °C,. Unfortunately, these two alloys had high density (>12 g/cm3) and further developments aimed at reducing the alloy density while keeping superior high-temperature properties. In the second generation RHEAs, high-density Ta and W were replaced with lower density refractory elements, such as Cr, Mo, Nb, V and Zr, and low density Al and Ti were added. This resulted in RHEAs with lower densities and high-temperature strengths better than the properties of Ni-based superalloys and Fe-based steels. Recently the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), consisting of four or more principle metallic elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratios, has attracted considerable interest owing to its tendency to form solid solution with outstanding mechanical and functional properties [,,,,,]. By introducing refractory elements including group IV (Ti, Zr, and Hf), V (V, Nb, and Ta), and VI (Cr, Mo, and W) in HEAs, the developed refractory HEAs (RHEAs) possess high melting temperature, outstanding strength and hardness, high thermal stability, and softening resistance at elevated temperatures, which opens up the possibilities of the alloy developments satisfying structural demands at high temperature.

The equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was chosen to analyze the effect of each constituent elemental by the subtraction method and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were studied. Among these alloys, HfMoNbTaTi has the best mechanical performance, that is, 27% compressive strain at room temperature and yield strength 367 MPa at 1400 °C. HfMoNbTaTi has great potential for elevated-temperature applications. As the alloy system does not contain very expensive elements such as Re and Ru, it is cost competitive for high-temperature applications like Nb-Hf-Ti alloys in space vehicles. Further modification of composition and/or anti-oxidation coatings are still required for high-temperature applications in the air. According to the experiment results, the effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on mechanical properties of equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr alloys were described. For higher room-temperature strength, one should add an element which interacts frequently with the alloy, such as Mo. The aim of the current work was to develop and design new RHEAs, which have low density and high strength at elevated temperature for high-temperature applications. The density of the Al0.8NbTiVM0.2 (M = Co, Ni) alloys was measured to be approximately 5.84 g cm−3, which is slightly larger density than the Al0.8NbTiV alloy (5.61 g cm−3) due to the addition of Co and Ni. However, this value is much lower than conventional high-temperature materials, such as Inconel 718 (8.22 g cm−3) [] and RHEAs. Most reported RHEAs possess high density of 6–13 g cm−3, i.e., NbTiVZr and CrNbTiVZr alloys are 6.52 and 6.57 g cm−3 [], respectively.
